lesson.menu_desc: Phase 4 -- give travel advice that sounds like it matters, with complex imperatives -- 38 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 32 -- Make Sure You... -- Complex Imperatives
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Mark Kazuyoshi Seki Omagari | Lesson 32 -- Make Sure You...
lesson.grammar_point: complex imperatives and instructions (make sure + present clause, be sure to, remember to and don't forget to + infinitive, whatever you do + negative imperative, emphatic do, never and always + imperative, and imperative + and/or + result)

listenings.text: Hi Mark. Last class you stood on a day that had not arrived yet and looked back at it. Today you do the next thing a trip needs, which is telling somebody else what to do. You already know the simple instruction. Take the train. Don't take a taxi. It works, but it is flat, and it gives every piece of advice exactly the same weight. English has a few ways to make an instruction heavier, and each one does a different job. Make sure, plus a full sentence, is for the one thing that must not go wrong. Make sure you keep your passport on you. And here is the first trap. After make sure, English uses the present, never will. Make sure you keep it, not make sure you will keep it. Be sure to, remember to and don't forget to all take the infinitive. Be sure to try the ramen. Don't forget to charge your phone. Whatever you do, don't, is the loudest warning the language has. Whatever you do, don't put your wallet in your back pocket. Use it once in a conversation, or it stops meaning anything. Then there is do, in front of a positive instruction, which sounds warm instead of bossy. Do try the bento at the station. And the last pattern hides a condition inside it. Leave before eight, or you will miss the fast train. Buy the pass on the first morning, and you will save money all week. Or means if you don't. And means if you do. The second trap is forget. Don't forget to buy the pass is an instruction about later. Don't forget buying it is not an instruction at all. The third trap comes from Portuguese. People say no touch, or not touch. In English a negative instruction starts with don't, or with never, and never with both. Before class, write five tips for somebody visiting Sao Paulo for the first time, with a different pattern in every one. See you in class, Mark.

Hello, and welcome in advance to Kamo River Hostel. This is Kenji, and this message goes to everybody arriving this week, so please listen to the end. First, the check-in. The front desk closes at ten at night. Whatever you do, don't arrive after ten without telling us, because the door locks and nobody will be here to open it. If your flight is late, send us a message, and we will leave a code for you. Second, the shoes. Take them off at the entrance and leave them on the shelf. The slippers are for the hallway only, so be sure to leave them outside the bathroom as well. Third, the kitchen. Do use it, because it is the best room in the house, but wash your own plates before you go to bed, or they will be in the sink with your name on them in the morning. The quiet hours start at eleven. The walls here are thin, so after eleven keep your phone calls for the garden. Now, getting around. Buy a transport card at the station on your first morning, and you will never have to think about tickets again. The buses are easy, but they are always full in the afternoon, so try to go out early. And one heads-up about money. A lot of small restaurants in Kyoto still take cash only, so make sure you have some on you before you leave in the morning. There is a machine at the convenience store on the corner. That is everything. If you have a question, the answer is probably on the board in the hall, and if it is not, ask me. See you soon.

extra_audio.text: The night before, double-check the flight time and the address of the hostel, because that is the last moment you can still fix a mistake calmly. In the morning, pack your carry-on last, with the charger, the plug adapter, your medicine and one change of clothes, so that nothing important is in the suitcase. Then leave for the airport early, or the check-in line will eat the extra hour you thought you had. On the plane, fill in the customs form before you land, and you will be out before the rest of the line. Finally, when you arrive, buy a transport card before you leave the station, and you will never have to think about tickets again.

reading.rtitle: Before You Land: A First-Timer's List for Japan
paras: Last summer one of our writers spent three weeks in Japan and came back with a notebook full of mistakes she made so that you do not have to. Here they are, in the order you will meet them. The first one happens before the plane has even left. Pack your carry-on as if the suitcase is going to disappear, because one day it will: a charger, a plug adapter, a change of clothes and anything you cannot replace. Whatever you do, don't put your medicine in the bag that goes in the hold.

When you land, you go through customs, and it is quicker than you think if the form is ready. Fill it in on the plane, and you will be out of the airport before the rest of the line. Then double-check the name of your hostel in Japanese characters and keep it on your phone, because a taxi driver cannot read an address he has never seen in English. Japan is one of the safest places in the world, and pickpockets are rare, but keep an eye on your bag in the big stations anyway. Rare is not the same as never.

Now the part nobody warns you about, which is etiquette. Take your shoes off whenever you see a step up at a door. Keep your voice down on the train, and never talk on the phone there at all. Do bow back when somebody bows to you, even a small bow; nobody expects it to be perfect. And don't leave a tip. In a restaurant it confuses people, and they will run after you to give it back. As a rule of thumb, if everybody around you is quiet, be quiet too.

Last, the money. Stock up on cash before you leave a big city, because small restaurants and temples in the countryside often take nothing else. Be sure to carry more than you think you need, just to be on the safe side. And steer clear of the exchange booths at the airport, where the rate is the worst in the country. Make sure you use a machine at a convenience store instead. That is the whole list. Follow it, and the only thing you will have to worry about is how much you can eat.
